groups.h: Selection in Python — if, elif, else
points: Selection lets a program choose a path. The full shape: `if condition:` → first choice, `elif another:` → tested only if everything above failed, `else:` → catches whatever's left. Each keyword line ends in a **colon**, each branch body is **indented**.

**The one-branch rule:** in an if/elif/else chain, exactly **one** branch runs — the first whose condition is True — and then Python skips the rest of the chain entirely. Even if a later condition would also have been True, it is never looked at.

That's why **order matters**. Grading with 70+ = A, 50+ = B: test `mark >= 70` FIRST. If you test `mark >= 50` first, a mark of 85 passes it, gets a B, and the A branch never gets a chance. Rule of thumb: **most specific / highest band first**. When a question says 'the program gives the wrong grade/price', wrongly-ordered conditions are the first thing to check.

**Separate `if` statements are different animals:** without `elif`, every `if` is tested independently, so several can fire. `if n > 10: print("Big")` followed by `if n > 15: print("Very big")` prints BOTH for n = 20. Use separate ifs only when several things can genuinely be true at once; use elif when the options are alternatives.

**Nested if** = an if inside an if; the inner test only happens when the outer passed. `if member:` containing `if spend > 50:` requires **both** — which is why it can be flattened to `if member and spend > 50:`. Exams ask for exactly this simplification.
groups.hook: ** *elif = 'else, if you're still here…'* — it only speaks when everything above has said no.

groups.h: for loops and range() — counting made automatic
points: `for i in range(…):` repeats a block a **known** number of times, managing the counter for you — which is why a for loop can never accidentally become infinite.

**The range rules (learn cold):** `range(5)` → 0,1,2,3,4 (starts at 0, FIVE values). `range(1, 5)` → 1,2,3,4 (stops **before** the second number — always one before!). `range(2, 11, 3)` → 2,5,8 (third number is the step). Counting down needs a negative step: `range(10, 0, -1)` → 10 … 1.
**To include N, write N+1:** printing 1 to 10 needs `range(1, 11)`. This 'stop is exclusive' rule is the most-tested fact in the whole chapter — planted off-by-one errors everywhere.
Traps: `range(10, 4)` produces **nothing** (can't count up from 10 to 4 with the default +1 step); `range(5, 5)` is empty; forgetting the -1 step on countdowns silently prints nothing.
`for` doesn't only count — it walks through things: `for c in "code":` visits each character (c, o, d, e); `for item in basket:` visits each list element. Reads as 'for each…', no counter needed.
**How many times does it run?** = how many values range produces. `range(4, 13, 4)` → 4, 8, 12 → three times. Listing the values on paper first is faster and safer than reasoning in your head.

`while condition:` repeats its body **while the condition stays True**, checking **before** every pass. Use it when the number of repetitions isn't known: validation, passwords, sentinel values, games.
Because the check comes first, a while loop can run **zero times**: `n = 8` then `while n > 8:` — the very first test fails, the body never runs. (Exam phrasing: 'a pre-condition loop'.)

**The infinite-loop rule:** something inside the body must push the condition towards False. `while i <= 5:` with no `i = i + 1` inside spins forever. Whenever an exam says 'this program never stops', look for the missing update line.

**Python has no REPEAT…UNTIL.** The must-run-at-least-once pattern is done two ways: read the input **once before** the loop (`n = int(input())` then `while invalid:` re-read inside), or `while True:` with a `break` when the exit condition is met. Both appear in real papers — recognise both.

Converting for ↔ while (a standard 3-marker): `for i in range(8):` becomes `i = 0` / `while i < 8:` / body / `i = i + 1`. Three ingredients: initialise before, test at the top, update inside. Forget the update and you've written the infinite-loop bug on purpose.
**Choosing for vs while in one line:** count known → for; count unknown/condition-based → while.

groups.h: Nested loops — a loop inside a loop
points: The rule that unlocks every nested-loop question: **the inner loop runs completely, start to finish, for every single pass of the outer loop.** Outer picks a row; inner sweeps all the columns of that row; outer moves to the next row.

So total body-executions = outer × inner: `for i in range(3):` containing `for j in range(4):` runs the innermost code **12** times. If asked 'how many times does print run?', multiply — then check whether any prints sit in the *outer* body only (those run just 'outer' times).

Tracing output order: hold the outer value fixed while the inner cycles. `range(2)` inside `range(2)` printing `i, j` gives 0 0, 0 1, 1 0, 1 1 — notice the left number 'sticks' while the right one spins. Write traces in a grid and the pattern is unmissable.

Where they appear: grids and seating plans (12 rows × 7 seats = 84 labels), times-table squares, repeated passes in sorting. A variable inner range (`for j in range(i):`) makes triangles — the inner count grows with i: 0+1+2 runs for i in range(3).
`break` inside the **inner** loop exits **only the inner** loop — the outer carries on with its next iteration. It never jumps out of both.

groups.h: break and continue — the loop escape hatches
points: `break` = *leave this loop right now*; execution jumps to the first line after the loop. Classic use: stop a search the instant the target is found — why keep comparing? (That's also the standard 'make it more efficient' answer.)
`continue` = *abandon this iteration only*; jump straight back to the loop's test and start the next pass. Classic use: skip items you want to ignore (blank survey answers) while continuing the loop.

Side-by-side to fix them in memory: in a loop over 1..9, `if i == 4: break` prints 1 2 3 and stops; `if i == 4: continue` prints 1 2 3 5 6 7 8 9 — only 4 goes missing. **break kills the loop, continue skips the lap.**

`while True:` + `break` is the legitimate 'repeat until' idiom — but the break must be reachable, or you've built an infinite loop. When reading `while True:` code, your first act is to find the break and ask *'can we always get there?'*
Style note exams reward: a clear loop condition beats a buried break when either would do — the condition documents when the loop ends; a break hides it.

groups.h: Boolean logic — and, or, not without tears
points: Python's logical operators are lowercase words: `and` (both sides must be True), `or` (at least one True), `not` (flips). Core truth facts: `True and False = False`; `True or False = True`; `not True = False`; `False or False = False`.

**Inside a range** uses and: `n >= 10 and n <= 20` (both fences must hold). **Outside a range** uses or: `n < 10 or n > 20` (breaking either fence is enough). Notice the flip — inverting an and-range produces an or-condition. Validation loops are the classic home of the or-version: `while day < 1 or day > 31: re-ask`.

**The always-True trap (a guaranteed exam question):** `if choice == "1" or "2":` does NOT test for 1-or-2. Python reads it as `(choice == "1") or ("2")`, and a bare non-empty string counts as True — so the condition passes for *everything*. Each side of `or`/`and` must be a **complete comparison**: `choice == "1" or choice == "2"`.

Its evil twin in loops: `while answer != "Y" or answer != "N":` loops **forever** — whatever answer is, it differs from at least one of the two, so the or is always True. Staying-in-the-loop conditions over several forbidden values need **and**: `while answer != "Y" and answer != "N":`.

**Brackets change meaning:** `and` binds tighter than `or`, so `key and torch or rope` means `(key and torch) or rope` — a player with just a rope sneaks through. Wanted: `key and (torch or rope)`. When combining and with or, always bracket your intention.

Evaluate complex conditions inside-out on paper: work out each comparison's True/False, then combine. `coins >= 100 and (choice == 1 or choice == 2) and stock > 0` with coins=120, choice=3, stock=5 → True and False and True → **False**.

groups.h: Choosing and combining constructs — design instincts
points: Read the task, underline the clue words: *'for each / exactly 12 / all items'* → **for** loop. *'until valid / keep asking / while there are'* → **while**. *'if / depending on / choose'* → **selection**. *'then'* → sequence. The wording of the question almost always names its own construct.

Alternatives that are mutually exclusive (grade bands, price tiers, medals) → one if/elif/else chain, most specific first. Conditions that can hold simultaneously (warnings, badges earned) → separate ifs.

Standard combinations to recognise instantly: **loop + if** = filtering/counting ('count the negatives'); **loop + running variable** = totals and maxima; **nested loops** = grids and tables; **while + validation condition** = re-ask until acceptable.

When converting between loop forms or simplifying nests, prove your rewrite with a 10-second trace on one example — equivalence claims are only worth marks if the behaviour truly matches (including the boundary value!).
**Chapter in one breath:** *elif picks one; range stops early; while checks first; inner finishes first; break kills, continue skips; and needs both, or needs one — and never bare-string an or.*
